claims.text: The starting W–Cu composite contains discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
The untreated W–Cu composite tends to undergo phase separation under high thermal and irradiation stress.
The untreated W–Cu composite develops interfacial voids under high thermal and irradiation stress.
A uniform nanoscale TiC dispersion can be incorporated specifically at the W–Cu interface by controlled compositional modification.
TiC particles at the interface pin grain boundaries and impede grain-boundary migration.
TiC particles act as barriers to atomic diffusion across the W–Cu interface.
Impeded grain-boundary migration and reduced interfacial diffusion suppress phase separation.
Impeded grain-boundary migration and reduced interfacial diffusion suppress interfacial void formation.
TiC stabilizes the W–Cu interface during thermal cycling and irradiation.
Maintaining interfacial microstructural integrity enhances the composite's thermal conductivity.
Relative to untreated W–Cu, TiC-modified W–Cu will exhibit fewer interfacial voids under equivalent service conditions.
Relative to untreated W–Cu, TiC-modified W–Cu will exhibit less phase separation under equivalent service conditions.
Relative to untreated W–Cu, TiC-modified W–Cu will have higher thermal conductivity under equivalent heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
Dispersed TiC is beneficial under high heat-flux conditions relevant to plasma-facing applications.
Dispersed TiC improves irradiation resistance in W-based plasma-facing materials.
The optimal TiC concentration and distribution for long-term stability during continuous irradiation and repeated thermal cycling are not established.
